from pytrends.request import TrendReq
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Start PyTrends session
pytrends = TrendReq(hl='en-US', tz=360)

# Batch A1: Aesthetics-focused
aesthetic_terms = ["six pack", "aesthetic body", "shredded physique", "fitness model workout", "how to get ripped"]

# Batch H1: Health-focused
health_terms = ["cardio health", "flexibility exercises", "functional fitness", "cardio time", "longevity fitness"]

# Run aesthetic terms
pytrends.build_payload(aesthetic_terms, timeframe='2004-01-01 2024-12-31')
aesthetic_df = pytrends.interest_over_time().drop(columns=['isPartial'])

# Run health terms
pytrends.build_payload(health_terms, timeframe='2004-01-01 2024-12-31')
health_df = pytrends.interest_over_time().drop(columns=['isPartial'])

# Save for later if needed
aesthetic_df.to_csv("../data/google_trends_aesthetic.csv")
health_df.to_csv("../data/google_trends_health.csv")

# Plot trends together
plt.figure(figsize=(14,6))

# Plot top 3 from each for clarity
for col in ["six pack", "aesthetic body", "shredded physique"]:
    plt.plot(aesthetic_df.index, aesthetic_df[col], label=f"Aesthetic: {col}", linewidth=2)

for col in ["cardio health", "flexibility exercises", "functional fitness"]:
    plt.plot(health_df.index, health_df[col], label=f"Health: {col}", linestyle="--", linewidth=2)

plt.title("Google Trends: Aesthetic vs Health-Oriented Fitness Goals (2004–2024)")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Search Interest (0–100)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("../visuals/google_trends_aesthetics_vs_health.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

📊 Google Trends Analysis: Aesthetics vs Health in Fitness (2004–2024)¶

This chart compares public interest over time for two categories of fitness goals:

  • Aesthetics-focused: "six pack", "aesthetic body", "shredded physique", "fitness model workout", "how to get ripped"
  • Health-focused: "cardio health", "flexibility exercises", "functional fitness", "cardio time", "longevity fitness"

🔍 Key Insights:¶

  1. Dominance of Aesthetic Goals:

    • "Six pack" searches far outpace all others, especially during 2010–2018, showing how aesthetics have historically led public interest in fitness.
    • Seasonal peaks indicate heightened visual motivation around summer months or new year goals.

  2. Low Visibility of Health-Centric Terms:

    • Terms like "cardio health" and "longevity fitness" remain consistently low, suggesting preventive health and long-term wellness are underprioritized in search behavior.

  3. Rise of Functional Fitness & Flexibility (Post-2020):

    • "Flexibility exercises" show a notable rise during and after the COVID-19 pandemic — possibly linked to at-home workout trends and a growing appreciation for mobility.
    • This could reflect a micro-shift in public awareness toward functional, longevity-oriented fitness — though not enough to challenge aesthetic dominance.

💡 Interpretation:¶

While there is a subtle rise in interest toward flexibility and functionality, the overwhelming trend still reflects a culture hyper-focused on appearance. In an environment where "aesthetic body" vastly outshines "cardio health," the pressure to look fit often overrides the goal to be healthy.

This insight ties directly into the next section of the project: the rise of performance-enhancing drug (PED) culture, where shortcuts to extreme physiques are increasingly normalized — regardless of the cost.

from pytrends.request import TrendReq
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Initialize PyTrends
pytrends = TrendReq(hl='en-US', tz=360)

# A2: Steroid/PED keywords
a2_terms = ["anavar", "trenbolone", "blast and cruise", "steroid cycle", "ripped fast"]

# H2: Longevity & health-performance keywords
h2_terms = ["HIIT for heart", "mobility training", "heart rate zones", "walk for health", "VO2 max"]

import time

# Get A2 data
pytrends.build_payload(a2_terms, timeframe='2004-01-01 2024-12-31')
a2_df = pytrends.interest_over_time().drop(columns=['isPartial'])

# Introduce a delay to avoid TooManyRequestsError
time.sleep(10)

# Get H2 data
pytrends.build_payload(h2_terms, timeframe='2004-01-01 2024-12-31')
h2_df = pytrends.interest_over_time().drop(columns=['isPartial'])

# Save if needed
a2_df.to_csv("../data/google_trends_steroids.csv")
h2_df.to_csv("../data/google_trends_health_advanced.csv")

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(14,6))

# Plot top A2 and H2 terms for visibility
for col in ["anavar", "trenbolone", "steroid cycle"]:
    plt.plot(a2_df.index, a2_df[col], label=f"PED: {col}", linewidth=2)

for col in ["HIIT for heart", "VO2 max", "mobility training"]:
    plt.plot(h2_df.index, h2_df[col], label=f"Health: {col}", linestyle='--', linewidth=2)

plt.title("Google Trends: PED Culture vs Health Performance Awareness (2004–2024)")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Search Interest (0–100)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("../visuals/google_trends_ped_vs_advanced_health.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

💉 Google Trends: PED Culture in Fitness (2004–2024)¶

This chart examines search interest in traditional performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) such as:

  • Anavar
  • Trenbolone
  • Steroid cycle

These substances are widely known within bodybuilding communities and are often associated with rapid muscle gain and extreme physique enhancement.

🔍 Key Insights:¶

  1. Searches for “anavar” and “trenbolone” show a sharp increase, particularly between 2012 and 2020.
  2. There are seasonal peaks and upward trends, possibly driven by transformation challenges, cutting seasons, or influencer exposure.
  3. The consistently high interest in "steroid cycle" suggests widespread curiosity about how to structure PED usage, especially among non-competitive lifters.

⚠️ Cultural Implication:¶

The normalization of steroid-related terms online suggests a broader acceptance of chemical enhancement in the pursuit of aesthetics — moving beyond elite bodybuilding into the mainstream. It's no longer niche; it's aspirational for many.

This rise in PED interest lays the foundation for even more accessible, experimental alternatives — which brings us to the next section: SARMs.

sarms_terms = ["sarms", "ostarine", "rad 140", "lgd", "mk 677"]

plt.title("Google Trends: SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) Popularity (2004–2024)")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Search Interest")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("../visuals/google_trends_sarms.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

🧪 Google Trends: SARMs – The New Wave of Performance Enhancement (2004–2024)¶

This chart explores the rising popularity of SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) — compounds such as:

  • sarms
  • ostarine
  • rad 140
  • LGD (Ligandrol)

Marketed as “safer” or “legal” alternatives to steroids, SARMs have become especially popular among teens and recreational lifters seeking dramatic results without the stigma or invasiveness of traditional PEDs.

🔍 Key Insights:¶

  1. The term “sarms” has seen a dramatic post-2015 spike, peaking during 2019–2022 — aligning with their boom on TikTok, YouTube, and Reddit.
  2. Compound-specific interest in “ostarine”, “rad 140”, and “LGD” highlights growing awareness, usage, and experimentation in mainstream fitness spaces.
  3. The trend mimics supplement cycles — quick spikes, persistent baseline curiosity, and recurring engagement — suggesting a shift in how these compounds are perceived.

🧠 Implication:¶

  • SARMs are blurring the line between “natural” and “enhanced,” especially in online communities that market them with minimal transparency.
  • Despite their legal ambiguity and lack of FDA approval, they’re being normalized — even among casual gym-goers and young audiences.

We're witnessing a decentralization of enhancement culture — it's no longer underground or elite, but repackaged for mass consumption.

The growing list of fitness influencers and athletes who died young — many with direct or indirect ties to performance-enhancing drugs.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Set style
sns.set(style="whitegrid")

# --- Plot 1: Deaths by Age Group ---
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.countplot(data=influencer_df, x='Age Group', order=['<30', '30–39', '40–49', '50–59', '60+'], palette='Reds')
plt.title('Number of Influencer Deaths by Age Group')
plt.xlabel('Age Group')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../visuals/deaths_by_age_group.png')
plt.show()

# --- Plot 2: PED Involvement Pie Chart ---
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
ped_counts = influencer_df['PED Category'].value_counts()
plt.pie(ped_counts, labels=ped_counts.index, autopct='%1.1f%%', colors=sns.color_palette('pastel'))
plt.title('PED Involvement in Deaths')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../visuals/ped_involvement_pie.png')
plt.show()

# Extract the year from the 'Date of Death' column
influencer_df['Year of Death'] = pd.to_datetime(influencer_df['Date of Death'], errors='coerce').dt.year


# --- Plot 3: Timeline of Deaths per Year ---
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
yearly_deaths = influencer_df['Year of Death'].value_counts().sort_index()
sns.lineplot(x=yearly_deaths.index, y=yearly_deaths.values, marker='o', color='black')
plt.title('Number of Influencer Deaths per Year')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Number of Deaths')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../visuals/deaths_per_year_timeline.png')
plt.show()

📊 Influencer Mortality Analysis¶

To quantify the real-world consequences of performance-enhancing drug culture in fitness, we analyzed a curated dataset of notable influencers and professional athletes who died prematurely.

1. Deaths by Age Group¶

The chart clearly shows that the majority of deaths occurred between ages 30 and 49, with a substantial number occurring even before 30. This is deeply concerning given these individuals were presumed to be in peak physical condition.

🔎 Insight: The pursuit of extreme aesthetics is claiming lives well before the average life expectancy, particularly in the early stages of adulthood.

2. PED Involvement Breakdown¶

The pie chart reveals that:

  • 75% of deaths were confirmed PED users
  • An additional 12.5% were suspected but unconfirmed
  • Only 12.5% had no known connection to enhancement drugs

💊 Insight: This validates the trend we observed earlier — PED usage isn't just correlated with extreme physiques; it's potentially linked to early mortality.

3. Deaths Over Time¶

The line plot demonstrates that fitness-related deaths have accelerated post-2015, coinciding with:

  • The rise of influencer-based fitness marketing
  • Increased accessibility to SARMs and steroids
  • Normalization of PED use on platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and Reddit

📈 Insight: We're witnessing a clear uptick in mortality in the social media era, where aesthetic perfection is broadcasted, monetized, and often chemically enhanced.

These charts close the loop on a critical question:

What happens when fitness stops being about health and becomes a high-stakes aesthetic competition?

The data speaks for itself.

✅ Notebook Summary: The Aesthetic Trap — From Trends to Tragedy¶

This notebook explored how the definition of "fitness" has shifted in modern culture — from health and performance to aesthetics and extremity.

📌 What We Uncovered:¶

  1. Gym Cost vs Income
    Gym memberships have inflated significantly over the years, outpacing median income growth — making fitness access itself a class issue.

  2. Search Trends: PEDs and SARMs
    Google Trends show a cultural shift toward physique enhancement over health, with growing interest in:

    • Steroids (e.g., anavar, trenbolone)
    • SARMs (e.g., ostarine, rad 140, LGD)
    • Performance-focused alternatives fading into background

  3. Normalizing Enhancement Culture
    SARMs are now treated like supplements, promoted by influencers, and discussed in “natural” bodybuilding forums — further blurring ethical and medical boundaries.

  4. Influencer Mortality Data
    A dataset of over 25 public figures shows a disturbing pattern:

    • Most died between ages 30–49
    • 75% had confirmed PED use
    • Spike in deaths post-2015 aligns with social media’s explosion and mass PED exposure

💡 Final Insight:¶

Fitness is no longer about living longer — it's about looking better, faster.

Social media, competitive culture, and chemical shortcuts have created a generation chasing an aesthetic standard that often comes at the cost of health, transparency, and even life.
